paras: Marta, an operations director from Chile: "The program, which I started at forty-four, was the first time in twenty years that I sat in a room with people who did not report to me. My learning team, whose members came from six countries, became my sounding board. The case that changed my mind was about a family company where the founder refused to step back. I had lived that case. I did not expect to see it from the outside, and it was eye-opening."

Daniel, an engineer from Canada: "I will be honest about the return on investment. The salary increase that people talk about did not happen for me, because I went back to the company that I already owned a stake in. What paid off was different. The peers I met in the second residency are the people I call when a project goes wrong. Three of them are now clients, and one of them is my closest friend."

Kenji, a hospital director from Japan: "The thing nobody tells you is that the network is a two-way street. The alumni who get the most from it are the ones who give first: an introduction, an hour on the phone, a firsthand answer about a market. The program lived up to what I was promised, but only because I treated it as a beginning, not as a certificate that I could put on a wall."

listenings.text: Every candidate tells me he has spoken to our alumni. Very few can tell me what an alumnus actually said. So when I ask about it, I am checking two things. First, did you really have the conversation, or did you read the testimonials on our website? The testimonials are fine, but they are written to sell. A real conversation always contains something the website does not say, something that surprised you or even worried you. Second, what did you do with it? If an alumna told you that the learning team was the hardest part of the program, I want to know how you are preparing for that. The best candidates quote one person, by name, and then tell me what changed in their plan because of that conversation.

People ask me whether the program was worth the money, and my answer is always the same. The part that paid off was not the part I paid for. The classes were good, and some of the professors were excellent. But the thing that changed my career was a man who sat next to me in the first residency, a hospital director from Lisbon whose problems were almost exactly the same as mine. For eighteen months he was my sounding board, and I was his. We still speak every month. The certificate is in a drawer somewhere. If you are thinking about applying, my advice is simple. Choose the program where the people in the room are the ones you want to learn from, not the one with the best ranking.
